section_summary: This section continues an account of Japan’s 1938–39 extra budget and then lists proposed obligations under special accounts. Later documents concern the sale of unregistered Japanese government bonds in the United States, a proposed American loan for an aircraft plant in Manchukuo, and Japan’s gold shipments. The section ends within a consular report calculating Japan’s foreign bond obligations and assessing its capacity to pay them.

subfiles.title: Extra Budget for 1938–39 Fiscal Year: General Account, continued
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists multiyear appropriations and subsidy commitments in Japan’s 1938–39 extra budget.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages continue schedules for harbor, road, shrine, government building, prison, education, and other construction projects. They then list annual allocations and contract authority for agricultural, fishing harbor, forestry, petroleum, export, shipping, and aviation subsidies. Page 166 identifies the following enclosure as belonging to the Embassy’s despatch of August 29, 1938.

subfiles.title: Extra Budget for 1938–39 Fiscal Year: Special Accounts
subfiles.about: Enclosure 8 summarizes contract authority and multiyear spending under Japan’s special accounts.
subfiles.summary: The schedules cover Foreign Affairs, Finance, Communications, Railways, and overseas administrations in Korea, Taiwan, and Karafuto. They authorize purchases, transport and civil engineering subsidies, rice storage support, export indemnification, and other commitments extending beyond 1938–39. Taiwan entries include a guarantee against bank losses on loans to monetary guilds serving Japanese residents in South China and the South Sea Islands.

subfiles.title: Sale of Japanese Government Bonds in the United States
subfiles.from: George C. Mathews, Acting Chairman, Securities and Exchange Commission
subfiles.about: The SEC seeks State Department comment before acting against an unregistered Japanese bond offering.
subfiles.summary: Mathews reports that J. Yonemoto and F. M. Nonaka, acting through the Japanese Heimusha Kai of America, solicited purchases of Japanese treasury bonds from groups in California and Utah. The SEC considers the bond sale and broker activity unlawful under U.S. securities statutes and asks for prompt State Department comment before seeking an injunction.

subfiles.title: Illegal Sale in the United States of Japanese Government Bonds
subfiles.about: State and SEC officials agree to warn the bond sellers before taking legal action.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck recommends a warning to Yonemoto and Nonaka, followed by legal action if their activities continue or are not undone. SEC officials accept that approach. After further consultation, both agencies agree that the Japanese Embassy need not be approached at that time; the final telephone call is dated September 16.

subfiles.title: Transmission of SEC Letter and Conversation Memorandum
subfiles.about: The Department sends the Embassy copies concerning illegal Japanese bond sales in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the SEC letter and State Department conversation memorandum for the Ambassador’s information.

subfiles.title: Gold Shipment to the United States
subfiles.about: The Bank of Japan reports a ¥20 million gold shipment bound for the United States.
subfiles.summary: Reports the October 10 shipment aboard the Kunika Maru.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Gold Shipment Telegram
subfiles.about: A paraphrase repeats the Embassy’s report of gold shipped to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrases the Bank of Japan’s notice of a ¥20 million shipment on the Kunika Maru.

subfiles.title: File Note on Financial Conditions in Japan
subfiles.about: The note points to an Osaka report on Japan’s weakened foreign credit.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references Makinson’s report describing scarce foreign loans and cash-based import trade.

subfiles.title: Possible American Loan for a Manchukuo Aircraft Plant
subfiles.about: Hornbeck considers a public statement discouraging American financing of a Japanese aircraft venture.
subfiles.summary: Urges renewed consideration of a statement disfavoring American participation in the reported aircraft plant loan.

subfiles.title: Japan Seeks Loan For Plane Plant
subfiles.about: A news report describes a Japanese proposal to borrow up to $45 million for an aircraft plant in Mukden.
subfiles.summary: Reports Maebara’s proposed loan, factory inspections, and requirement that commercial planes be convertible for wartime use.

subfiles.title: Protest Against a Loan for a Japanese Aircraft Factory
subfiles.from: Signers at Indian Mountain School, Lakeville, Connecticut
subfiles.about: The signers ask the State Department to prevent or discourage financing for a Japanese aircraft factory.
subfiles.summary: The signers fear that planes made with American-financed machinery would be used against China or the United States. A postscript argues that national and humanitarian interests should prevail over those of an industrial concern.

subfiles.title: Review of Vice Consul White’s Bond Report
subfiles.about: Officials recommend removing speculative sections from White’s report before distribution.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum challenges White’s treatment of gold shipments, trade balances, exports, imports, and national debt, recommending deletion of part of page 24 and pages 29–43. A handwritten comment agrees but suggests retaining material on interest charges relative to revenue.

subfiles.title: The Status of Japan’s Dollar and Sterling Bonds
subfiles.from: Ivan B. White, American Vice Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: White estimates Japan’s foreign-held bond debt and the exchange needed for its 1939 payments.
subfiles.summary: White surveys national, municipal, and corporate foreign currency bonds, estimating ¥1.588 billion held abroad and about ¥125.7 million needed for 1939 interest, sinking funds, and redemption of an Osaka loan. Tables trace issue amounts, ownership, maturities, payments, and market prices. He then assesses gold shipments, export receipts, import needs, and Japan’s ability to service foreign debt. This section ends mid-report during his discussion of armament-related imports and industrial employment.
